title: Fly over Tarbela, the giant on the Indus
credits: 3D terrain: AWS Terrain Tiles · Imagery: Sentinel-2 cloudless 2016 by EOX (CC BY 4.0) · Map: Natural Earth
lines: On the Indus River, about one hundred and thirty kilometres north-west of Islamabad, stands one of the largest dams on Earth.
Let's fly up the Indus, towards Tarbela.
The river here flows out of the dam's spillways and power tunnels, on its way south across Pakistan.
And there it is: Tarbela Dam, completed in nineteen seventy-six, as part of the Indus Basin Project.
It is one of the world's largest earth- and rock-filled dams. Its crest stretches about two point seven kilometres.
Its main wall rises more than one hundred and forty metres above the riverbed.
Behind it lies Tarbela Lake, about eighty-one kilometres long, covering some two hundred and fifty-nine square kilometres.
The reservoir stores Indus water for Pakistan's farms, which depend on the river to grow wheat, cotton and rice.
Its power station has fourteen generating units, built in stages through tunnels in the dam, and more are being added.
Let's climb higher, and look back at the whole reservoir, with the dam far below.
For Pakistan, Tarbela is both a water bank and a powerhouse, and a symbol of how much the country depends on the Indus.
